Eli ei kysellä vastavalmistuneilta, vaan jo sellaisilta valmistuneilta, joilla on jo hieman työuraa takana. Tämä tehdään joka vuosi, eli vuosittain seurataan tilannetta ja kyselyssä kysytään paljon kaikenlaista ihan työllistymiseen liittyvää asiaa, että minkälainen on työmarkkinastatus, minkälainen työpaikka, työnantajan sektori. Kysytään siis paljon tällaista laadulliseen työllistymiseen liittyvää asiaa, koska tosiaan Tilastokeskushan seuraa esimerkiksi työllisyyden kehittymistä, mutta se on pelkkää numerodataa. Se ei kerro, että minkä tyyppistä se työllistyminen on. Meitä kiinnostaa myös nähdä se, että minne yliopistosta valmistuneet työllistyvät ja minkä tyyppistä se työ on. Ja kun sanoin tuossa aikaisemmin, että mielekästä, niin itse tietysti näen, että mielekästä työllistyminen on silloin, kun se ihminen on työllistynyt koulutustaan vastaaviin tehtäviin. Että jos työskentelee maisterin tutkinnolla ravintolakokkina, niin ei välttämättä ole kauhean mielekästä. Toki sille yksilöllehän se voi olla, että ihan hyvä uravalinta. Mutta tällaisia asioita. Siellä kysytään työttömyydestä vähän, seurataan myös sitä, mutta siitä kysellään vähän vähemmän. Ja kysytään myös sitten osaamisesta. Tuossa jo aikaisemmin Arttukin mainitsi tästä osaamisesta, että se on korkeakoulutetuille tärkeä asia tunnistaa sitä omaa osaamistaan ja päästä hyödyntämään sitä. Se on myös yksi meidän kyselyn keskiössä oleva asia.

# Tekijä: ecarver@helsinki.fi

Julkaistu 9 lokakuun, 2025 9 lokakuun, 2025

## 52. International Student Advisors at Uni.Helsinki. Cari Monroe and Larissa Vanamo

What do the International Student Advisors do at the University of Helsinki? Why did the university decide to establish such a role? What kind of tasks do the advisors currently have? How does International Student Advisor role fit in with the wider student services and guidance role of teachers and researchers? What is the International Student Advisor experience like for the students who they advise and the advisors themselves? Do international students have some needs that differ from the Finnish students?

The guests on the fourth episode of the fourth season of the Student Guidance at University podcast are International Affairs Specialist Larissa Vanamo and International Student Advisor Cari Monroe from the University of Helsinki Admissions and Student Advice unit. Monroe is also studies at University of Helsinki in the Master’s Programme in Environmental Change and Global Sustainability.

This is the first episode of this podcast in English. The official name of this podcast is Opiskelijoiden ohjaus yliopistossa and all the previous 51 episodes are in Finnish. You can find the previous episodes and the text transcripts of these episodes at this blog page.

## Listen to the episode at Soundcloud

## Episode transcript

The topic for the 52nd episode and fourth episode of the fourth season of the Student Guidance at University podcast is International Student Advisors at University of Helsinki. The guests for are International Affairs Specialist Larissa Vanamo and International Student Advisor Cari Monroe from the University of Helsinki Admissions and Student Advice unit.

The episode and transcript were published on October 9, 2025. The episode is 49 minutes long.

Eric Carver: Welcome to the Student Guidance at University podcast. This podcast examines issues and topics related to guidance of students and doctoral researchers at universities. My name is Eric Carver, and I’m the host of this podcast. I work as a specialist in strategic services for teaching at the University of Helsinki. I’m also currently working as a part-time university lecturer at the University of Jyväskylä in the guidance team at the Department of Teacher Education. I’m also starting a doctoral dissertation at the University of Eastern Finland, focusing on student guidance issues, which I hope to do alongside my work. This is the first episode I do in English. I have thought about it before, but it’s the very first time. So some information for first-time listeners. The official name of this podcast is opiskelijoiden ohjaus yliopistossa, and all the previous 51 episodes are in Finnish. You can find the previous episodes and the text transcripts of those episodes from the blog page of this podcast. The guests on the fourth episode of the fourth season of Student Guidance at University podcast are international affairs specialist Larissa Vanamo and international student advisor Carrie Munro from the University of Helsinki Admissions and Students Advice Unit. Munro also studies at University of Helsinki in the master program in environmental change and global sustainability. Welcome to the podcast, Larissa and Carrie.

Larissa Vanamo: Thank you so much for having us.

Eric Carver: In this episode, we’ll talk about the work that international student advisors do at the University of Helsinki. Why did the university decide to establish such a role? What kind of tasks do the advisors currently have? How does the international student advisor role fit in with the wider student services and guidance role of teachers and researchers? What is the international student advisor experience like for the students who they advise and the advisors themselves? Do international students have some needs that differ from Finnish students? What does the future look like for international student advisors? A lot of ground to cover there. Let’s start from the background of the whole thing. So Larissa, can you start by talking about the history and background of international student advisors at University of Helsinki? When did the university decide to establish such a role and why?

Larissa Vanamo: Sure, thank you Erik. So, the service was launched in spring 2023. Before that we didn’t have any targeted or specified students for international degree students. We had a housing quota for them and a service address for tuition fees and scholarships, but otherwise we did not have much of anything that would be specifically for international students. Then back in 2022, we did a service path project at the University of Helsinki, which was especially was researching, how is it going with our international students, what are the needs, and how can we make the service path smoother for them? There we got a lot of feedback from both students and staff, saying that we need a targeted service for international degree students, that they need face to face services, not just an email address because they want encounters, and they really want to feel that there’s someone there for them. So, through this project, and also through the talent boost funding at the time, we had enough leverage to then start the service and convince the leadership that it’s really needed. Then at the same time, we were inspired by the universities in Germany, or in this case in Berlin, who make use of international students in general, they hire students, and they have a lot of campus jobs. So, it’s a very common phenomenon there. So, we decided there was a need for this service for international students. We have this example from Germany, so why do we not just hire our own international degree students to do the job, thinking that most likely they would be the best to know the needs of the international degree students. So, then the service was launched in spring 2023. We did it so that we have one staff year, that is divided into four. So, we have four international degree students, each working 25 percent. We do that on purpose. So, we want to have four different persons with four different skill sets, cultural backgrounds, and personalities. So far, it has worked really well. We have three different service channels. We have the email address, desk shifts in the Kaisa house, and Zoom, which is also available upon request. What is also really relevant is that we develop the service together with the international advisors. So, it’s not me or anyone saying from the top down that this is how we should do it, but we’re all the time doing it together and asking everyone’s opinions and checking out what is going on with the international students.

Eric Carver: That is interesting. Carrie, you have been working in this role for quite some time. What kind of tasks do the international student advisors currently have? What do you actually do?

Cari Monroe: That’s a good question. Yes, I have been in this role for almost a year and a half now. I would say that we have a lot of different roles. It depends on the time of year what maybe we have more inquiries about, but essentially, our primary role is to be a support for international students. So, we are usually the first point of contact when an international student has any type of question. Administratively we deal a lot with tuition fees and scholarships because a lot of our target group are non-EU students who have tuition fee liability, which means they either pay tuition or they have a scholarship. So, those students usually have more questions about administrative things, and obviously there is a lot more pressure that comes along with that because there’s more at stake for these students. So, they usually have a lot more questions and want to make sure they really understand how to do their studies and make sure that everything is on track. We sometimes serve a little as a therapist role, especially at the Kaiser desk. A lot of students come and maybe do not have a specific question, but they are struggling in certain points of their life, and they just want someone who has been through it or can empathize a little bit in what the experience is as an international person in Finland because it can be quite challenging for a lot of people, especially students, as I said, who have a little bit more pressure financially, or students who come with their families. So, there is a lot that we cover. As it is September now, we just finished the wave of all the incoming students, so there is a lot of support and guidance we give on how to register with the authorities, and what are the first steps you have to do when you come here to register yourself in Finland. There are quite a lot of steps that you have to do as an international person moving here, as I am sure you know. There are not a lot of helpful resources online, so things are very confusing. So, we are here to answer questions. We did quite a lot of webinars and went in person to a lot of programs during their orientation weeks and gave some presentations about who we are, but also what you have to do right now. What are your priorities as an international student. I do not know, Larissa, if you have anything else to add.

Larissa Vanamo: No, that was very well covered.

Eric Carver: There is a lot of work. Some of that will follow the academic year and the dues for the academic year, and some are more related to the experience of being an international student.

Cari Monroe: Yeah, well said.

Eric Carver: So, how does the international student advisor role fit in with the wider student advice and guidance services, and also the guidance that is given by the teachers and the researchers? Larissa, maybe you can answer this first.

Larissa Vanamo: Yeah. So, I think the service complements really well the services we already have. So, for example, a student advisor can advise how to register as an attending student, extend the study rights, or you can have an education coordinator that can guide in the contents of the degree, or a teacher who can say what is the completion timetable of the course and how can you complete it, but the moment you add in the equation to tuition fees or scholarships and something goes wrong in that, that is when we are definitely needed. So, as Carrie said, a lot of the questions concern tuition fees and scholarships. It is something that I think the legal system in Finland is not prepared for having tuition fees and scholarships. There is a wealth of problems with immigration that the students cannot do anything about and that the university cannot do anything about, but which then really affects the students, the administration, and the programs. So we give a lot of support regarding these topics. In general, because we want to attract international students here, then we also have the responsibility to accommodate to their needs. We cannot just say hey, come here, this is the best place to study, but then expect them to just adjust to the Finnish education system without giving them extra support to manage here. So, I think the most important task is to support them, so that the students can play in an equal field with the domestic students in the end. It is wrong to expect them to just come here and manage just as well as the Finnish students, when actually just getting here can be quite complicated, and there are a lot of other hurdles at the beginning of the studies, such as a different culture, knowing your way around, and knowing how things work.

Eric Carver: Is there something you want to add, Carrie?

Cari Monroe: I was thinking also in terms of what Larissa said, I think we fit in really well with other support, in terms of we work quite a lot with education coordinators of the programs, and I do not think it should be, or is, the responsibility of a student to know which person kn

Essential Checklist for New International Students – International Committee HYY

# Essential Checklist for New International Students

Written using Gemini AI Chat.

Before You Arrive (3-6 Months Before):

- Admission & Visa (Research Start 4 Months Before):

- Double-check your admission letter for deadlines and required documents (originals & translations may be needed).
- Apply for a residence permit at least 4 months before your arrival (earlier for peak seasons) through the Finnish Immigration Service website (https://migri.fi/en/home). 

- Research specific permit type needed for your study program duration.
- Gather required documents like a valid passport, proof of financial support (bank statements, scholarships), and health insurance documents.
- Purchase health insurance that meets Finnish requirements. The University of Helsinki website offers guidance on acceptable plans. 

- Consider coverage for repatriation, dental care, and vision, as these may not be standard.
- Accommodation (Research & Apply 3-6 Months Before):

- Explore student housing options: 

- Apply for student housing through Unicato (foundation for student housing): https://hyy.fi/en/oppaat/housing/ (applications open typically in spring for fall semester and fall for spring semester).
- Research private rental options on websites like https://www.vuokraovi.com/?locale=en or Facebook groups. Apply well in advance as competition is high.
- Research average rental costs per area in Helsinki (e.g., Kallio, Töölö) to budget accordingly.
- Understand basic Finnish rental terms like “vuokrasopimus” (rental agreement) and “vesi- ja sähkömaksu” (water and electricity charges). You can find English translations online.
- Finances (Start Budgeting 3 Months Before):

- Research average living expenses in Helsinki for students (accommodation, food, transportation, course materials).
- Budget accordingly and factor in potential unexpected costs.
- Open a Finnish bank account online before arrival through banks like Nordea, Danske Bank, or OP. This simplifies receiving payments and managing finances.
- Research scholarship opportunities offered by the University of Helsinki (https://www.helsinki.fi/en/admissions-and-education/apply-bachelors-and-masters-programmes/tuition-fees-and-scholarship-programme) or external organizations (https://www.studyinfinland.fi/scholarships). Apply well before deadlines.
- Flights & Transportation (Research & Book 2-3 Months Before):

- Book your flights considering arrival dates for student orientation and potential accommodation move-in dates.
- Research airport transportation options (e.g., Finnair City Bus, train) from Helsinki Airport (VAN) to your accommodation (check journey times and costs).
- Consider purchasing a Helsinki Region Travel Card (HSL) online or upon arrival (https://www.hsl.fi/en/tickets-and-fares). This provides access to public transportation within Helsinki, Espoo, Kauniainen, and Vantaa. Explore different zones and validity periods to match your needs.
- Documentation (Prepare 3 Months Before):

- Pack important documents in a secure folder: passport, visa, admission letter, health insurance documents, academic transcripts (originals & translations may be required).
- Consider getting an International Student Identity Card (ISIC) for potential discounts on travel, accommodation, and cultural activities.

Upon Arrival (First Week):

- Registration & Residence Permit:

- Register with the Finnish authorities within 7 days of arrival (instructions provided by Finnish Immigration Service).
- Activate your residence permit card at a police station.
- University Orientation (Pre-register & Attend):

- Pre-register for the University of Helsinki’s international student orientation program (offered typically before semesters begin). This provides essential information and support.
- Familiarize yourself with the campus (check a campus map online) and locate key facilities like student services, libraries, and your department building.
- Collect your student ID card, which grants access to university facilities and discounts.
- Phone & Internet (Set Up Within the Week):

- Purchase a Finnish SIM card for your phone from operators like Elisa, Telia, or DNA. Explore prepaid or contract plans based on your needs.
- Arrange internet access for your accommodation. Many student housing options provide pre-installed internet connections. If renting privately, discuss internet options with your landlord.
- Bank Account & HSL Card (Set Up Within the Week):

- Visit your chosen bank to activate your bank account and get your debit card.

Arrival at Aalto University | Aalto University

# Arrival at Aalto University

 Information on arrival at Aalto University for incoming exchange students 

## Table of contents 

## Planning your arrival 

Read this part once you have been accepted for exchange by Aalto University

### Letter of Admission 

When you have been accepted for exchange studies by Aalto University you will receive a Letter of Admission by email. They will be sent by mid-June for students arriving for the autumn term and late November for students arriving for the spring term. Each Aalto school has their own process and timeline for sending them.

### Orientation and start of studies 

You should plan to arrive by the start of orientation. Attending orientation is mandatory for all exchange students, and you will receive all the information you need to start your studies smoothly. Your exchange coordinator will send you the orientation schedule that applies to exchange students at your Aalto school. Some orientation events are school-specific, so please follow the schedule given to you and attend the orientation of your Aalto school.

Teaching will start on the week following orientation. You can view the academic calendar for the exact dates of each teaching period.

### Non-EU/EEA citizens: residence permit or mobility notification 

Please apply for the residence permit immediately after receiving the Letter of Admission. It may take time for your application to be processed. Visit the website of the Finnish Immigration Service (Migri) for Instructions for exchange students. Please note that the electronic Letter of Admission is accepted in all Finnish embassies.

If you have a valid residence permit for studies issued by another EU country, you can also check if you meet the requirements for a mobility notification to Finland.

While applying for the residence permit, please note that you can ask to be registered in the Finnish Population Information System and to receive a Finnish personal identity code. This is highly recommended as the Finnish personal identity code will help you with many practicalities in Finland. 

Exchange students at Aalto University do not receive the National Learner ID number asked in the application. You can apply for a residence permit without it.

### EU/EEA citizens: registering right of residence 

EU/EEA, Switzerland and Liechtenstein citizens do not need a residence permit, instead they register their right of residence at the Finnish Immigration Service. The registration is required if you are staying in Finland for over 90 days without leaving the country. You can also obtain the Finnish personal identity code in connection with the registration.

You can fill in the online application once your study right has started and then book the appointment to visit the service point in Helsinki. The Finnish Immigration Service point in Helsinki is very busy and when you book an appointment, the next available time may be several weeks or even a few months away. 

You can watch this video on how to fill in the application form in Enter Finland 

From Migri's Frequently Asked Questions: 

I am an EU citizen and studying in Finland for six months. If I visit Estonia twice during the six months, do I need to register my right of residence in Finland? 

You do not need to do so if you do not stay in Finland without a break for over three months. If, for example, you arrive in Finland in January and travel outside Finland in March and May, you do not need to register your residence. Keep the receipt or tickets of your journey, in case you need to prove later that you travelled abroad.

### Nordic citizens: notifying move to Finland 

Nordic citizens do not need to register when staying in Finland for at most six months. If you intend to live in Finland for more than six months, you must visit the Digital and population data services agency (DVV) service location personally so that your information can be registered. 

See DVV's website for information on Moving between the Nordic countries. 

Nordic citizens do not need to complete EU/EEA citizen's registration at Finnish Immigration Service (Migri). 

### Insurance and health care 

Students must personally cover the costs if they become ill, therefore you must have sufficient insurance that is valid for the whole duration of your stay in Finland. Please note that exchange students do not have access to Finnish Student Health Services (FSHS).

If you need to apply for the residence permit (non-EU/EEA citizens), you must take out private insurance that covers medical and drug expenses. For more information, please see Migri’s website on insurance.

EU/EEA citizens must take the European Health Insurance Card (EHIC) with them to Finland. By presenting the European Health Insurance Card, you can prove the right to medically necessary treatment in Finland. The card must be valid for the whole duration of your exchange. We strongly recommend purchasing private health insurance as well, because it is significantly easier and faster to make an appointment at a private clinic. 

More information about Health care for exchange students.

### Accommodation 

Please note that you need to apply for housing yourself, see the instructions at Housing for exchange students. Aalto University does not own any student dormitories. The main student housing providers for Aalto’s students are HOAS and AYY.

Housing offers are sent via email, so it is important to check your inbox frequently after submitting a housing application. If you receive an offer from HOAS or AYY, we recommend you accept it even if the type or location is not exactly what you wished for. If you refuse an offer, it is very unlikely you will receive another offer.

When accepting the housing offer, please note that rental agreements with student organisations are often made for the whole term or whole academic year depending on your exchange study period. Please note that fixed-term contracts cannot be terminated before the end date of the contract. Make sure to read the terms and conditions of the housing offer before you accept it, you are responsible for the commitment you make. If you cancel your exchange, please remember to also cancel your housing applications.

If you prefer, you can arrange your accommodation through other channels. Just note that rental prices at the private market here in the Helsinki region are rather high. Although most of the private landlords are completely reliable, it’s good to keep in mind that there might be scammers posting ads that offer accommodation.

### Student tutors 

All exchange students are allocated student tutors who will help you at the beginning of the exchange with practical questions related to student life and arriving in Finland. All study-related questions should be sent to your exchange coordinator instead.

Tutoring is organized in co-operation with AYY, Student Guilds and Student associations. All tutors are volunteers and students of Aalto University. Tutors will contact you by email. Please be patient while waiting for the tutor’s email!

### Studies 

Your exchange coordinator will inform you of all the matters related to your studies, including course practicalities, school-specific guidelines, and Learning Agreement (Erasmus+ students) or study plan. Follow the instructions from your exchange coordinator, as there may be differences between Aalto schools.

### Financial arrangements 

What to take into consideration when planning your exchange:

- how to pay your rent and other possible bills (for example electricity and home insurance), these payments need to be made to the bank account and cannot be paid in cash
- card payments are most common method of payment in shops, some places don’t accept cash anymore
- cashier services in banks are limited (specific branches)
- some students use an internet bank (eg. Revolut, N26)
- opening a bank account in Finland can take a long time and unfortunately not all banks will give it for exchange students who are in Finland only for a few months
- living costs are rather high, please reserve sufficient budget for your stay, see examples on monthly costs

Checklist for Planning your arrival at Aalto University, pdf, attachment

## Preparing for the start of your studies 

Read this part approx. 4 weeks before the start of your exchange

### Aalto IT account 

You will receive an activation email - Welcome to Aalto University! – when your digital identity is created. You need to activate your digital identity to get the username and password.

Exchange students can activate user accounts without strong authentication (strong authentication means Finnish online banking ID or an ID card issued by the Finnish police). Registration is done by using the personal registration link in your activation email, with your email address and mobile phone number in international format. If you notice that your mobile phone number or name is incorrect, please contact your Aalto school’s exchange coordinator. Sometimes there are other issues with the activation, in which case please contact Aalto IT services. 

Once you have activated your Aalto IT account, you can access Aalto services including Aalto email, and login to Sisu.

### Enrolment and updating your personal information 

You will be automatically enrolled as attending for the duration of your exchange studies. You can download a Certificate of Student Status in Sisu which proves your attendance at Aalto University (this document is requested by Finnish authorities; they may refer to it as Certificate of Attendance).

In Sisu you can also check your personal information. Please remember to update them as needed (for example your address in Finland). If there is something you cannot update yourself, please contact your exchange coordinator.

### AYY membership 

Membership of the Student Union AYY is voluntary for exchange students but recommended. Please note that AYY housing offer is only possible to students who are members of the AYY Student Union and have paid the membership fee. As a member you are entitled to many benefits and only members can activate the digital Finnish student card (Frank). It is useful in Finland because with the Frank app you can get all the student benefits and discounts.

If you want to join the AYY you will need to pay the AYY membership fee. The payment instructions will be sent to you by your exchange coordinator at your Aalto school, so please wait to receive the instructions. You can fill in the AYY housing application with your admission letter even if you have not paid the membership fee yet. Once you have paid the fee, send the receipt to Aalto student services at studentservices@aalto.fi, and your membership payment will be updated into Sisu. Note that it may take a few days – only after this you can access Finnish student card FRANK.

### Webinars and emails before arrival 

Make sure to check your email regularly for more information from your exchange coordinator, specific to your Aalto school. Some schools arrange webinars for exchange students before the orientation week, where you get more information and can ask questions from the exchange coordinator. 

### Personal study plan and course registrations in Sisu 

Please follow the instructions from your Aalto school’s exchange coordinator before registering for courses and if you want to make changes to your Learning Agreement / Study plan. There might be limitations and you may not be able to choose all your preferred courses. Due to school-specific practices, it’s very important to follow the instructions of your Aalto school, given by your exchange coordinator. Please note that including a course in your plan does not guarantee a place on the course, you will need to register for it in Sisu and be accepted.

sources.title: Your first student week in Finland: housing, registration and starting university | Nordic Immigration
highlights:
## Before travelling: three arrangements for a smoother arrival

Save your key collection time, accommodation address and handover contact somewhere you can open offline. If you arrive outside office hours, agree the collection arrangements with your housing provider beforehand. Your flight landing time is not your arrival time at the apartment: allow for ground transport and possible delays.

Read your university’s new-student instructions separately from the admission letter. Make a short list of enrolment deadlines, orientation, account activation and the contact for access problems. If you are still planning, compare the budget for starting student life with travel expenses.

## Arrival day: housing and essential access first

- After collecting keys, inspect and document the room, supplied equipment and existing defects.
- Find the fault-reporting process, building internet instructions and household rules.
- Separate first-night essentials from large purchases and longer-term commitments.

For example, Helsinki-region housing provider Hoas asks tenants to submit a move-in report in MyHoas. The report is available for ten days from the tenancy start date; faults requiring repairs need a separate report. Do not apply that deadline to every landlord. Compare the official Hoas move-in instructions with your own agreement. Our Hoas housing guide and rental contract and deposit guide cover the earlier housing decisions.

## Starting university: accounts and orientation

Prioritise account activation, completing enrolment and finding the term’s starting programme. Admission, registration as an attending student and course registration serve different purposes. Your own institution’s instructions determine which steps remain outstanding.

If access fails, describe the error and the point where you became stuck to university support rather than creating duplicate accounts. Keep starting instructions, necessary letters and receipts in a secure personal folder. Do not post identity documents in a public student group.

## Registration: an identity code is not the same as a registered address

Henkilötunnus

 means a Finnish personal identity code. You may already have received one during your residence-permit process. Having the code does not by itself establish that your address and 

kotikunta

, or municipality of residence, have all been registered. Check your own situation against university and DVV instructions.

The University of Helsinki’s registration guide illustrates how steps differ by citizenship. For LUT and LAB, the general eLUT guidance describes campus registration events, so check your intake’s arrangements before booking a separate appointment. See eLUT’s practical services guide. This article does not promise that registration or an identity code will be completed during your first week.

## Banking, transport and health: allow for dependencies

Before visiting a bank, ask your chosen branch about required documents and appointments. Do not assume an account application, receiving a card and obtaining electronic identification are one immediate step. eLUT also notes that banking procedures vary. Test the route between home and campus before classes begin, and check student-discount conditions with your local transport provider.

Find the student healthcare pathway through your university and the FSHS guide for international students. Bring necessary health information and prescriptions for your own use, and check university enrolment and your access to services. Residence-permit insurance is a separate subject, explained in our student insurance guide.
